core: The paramountcy principle: engineering codes rank the safety, health, and welfare of the public above obligations to client and employer

The standing duties in the codes: competence and practising only in one's area, truthfulness in reports and testimony, disclosure of conflicts of interest, confidentiality and its limits, and sustainability obligations
The distinction between ethics, legality, and civil liability, and the fact that codes are enforced by state licensing boards and professional societies rather than by courts
What to do when the public-safety duty collides with organizational pressure: internal escalation, written documentation, the ethics of dissent
Whistleblowing as a last resort, with an honest account of the personal cost and of the patchwork, deadline-bound nature of legal protection

The standard case literature read against the investigations rather than the folklore: Challenger (Rogers Commission), Hyatt Regency walkways (NBS BSS 143), Ford Pinto (NHTSA recall and Grimshaw), Ford/Firestone (NHTSA and the TREAD Act), Volkswagen diesel emissions (EPA and DOJ)
Separating what investigations established from what remains contested
supporting: The stakeholder ordering in the ASCE code and the code's own disclaimer that it does not set a standard of care
OSHA's administration of anti-retaliation provisions under 23 federal statutes and the 30-day filing deadline under OSH Act section 11(c)
The structural pattern shared by the case studies: a known technical concern travelling upward through a decision structure with non-technical incentives
outOfScope: Licensure mechanics, the FE/PE exam path, ABET accreditation, and the structure of the profession — owned by engineering-fundamentals:engineering-thinking:what-engineers-do
Technical failure analysis, factors of safety, fracture and fatigue mechanics — owned by engineering-fundamentals:engineering-practice:safety-factors-and-failure
Legal advice, professional advice, or any position on a currently contested controversy
Reproduction of code text from NSPE, ASCE, IEEE, or any other copyrighted professional code
Moral philosophy survey (deontology vs. consequentialism) beyond what the codes themselves require

claims.claim: The first fundamental canon of the NSPE Code of Ethics for Engineers directs engineers to hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public, while a separate canon directs them to act as faithful agents or trustees for each employer or client; the code's own ordering makes the public duty the one that outranks the other.

The ASCE Code of Ethics lists five stakeholder groups in priority order — society, the natural and built environment, the profession, clients and employers, and peers — and states that protecting the health, safety, and welfare of the public takes precedence over every other responsibility in the code.

The ASCE Code of Ethics states in a footnote that the code does not establish a standard of care and should not be interpreted as one, which keeps professional-conduct rules distinct from the negligence yardstick a court applies.

Engineering codes require competence limits (undertaking assignments only when qualified by education or experience, and not sealing documents in subject matter one lacks competence in), objective and truthful professional reports and testimony that include all relevant and pertinent information, disclosure of known or potential conflicts of interest, and confidentiality of a client's or employer's business affairs and technical processes.

Confidentiality under the NSPE code is bounded rather than absolute: disclosure authorized or required by law or by the code itself is carved out, and engineers with knowledge of an alleged code violation are directed to report it to appropriate professional bodies and, when relevant, to public authorities.

Sustainability appears in current codes with different force: the NSPE code encourages adherence to the principles of sustainable development in a professional-obligation clause with an accompanying definition, while the ASCE code makes the natural and built environment its second-ranked stakeholder with obligations to adhere to sustainable development, balance societal, environmental, and economic impacts, mitigate adverse effects, and use resources wisely.

When an engineer's judgment is overruled under circumstances that endanger life or property, the NSPE code directs the engineer to notify the employer or client and such other authority as may be appropriate; it also directs engineers not to complete, sign, or seal plans or specifications that do not conform to applicable engineering standards, and, if a client or employer insists, to notify the proper authorities and withdraw from the project. The ASCE code similarly directs engineers to present the consequences clearly and promptly when engineering judgment is overruled where public health, safety, and welfare may be endangered.

Professional societies enforce their codes through membership sanctions, but the authority that can end a licensee's right to practise belongs to state and territorial licensing boards, which adopt and enforce their own rules of professional conduct; the NSPE code itself notes that state registration board rules of professional conduct remain in full force and effect, and NCEES describes licensure as a state-board mechanism for ensuring practice that protects public health, safety, and welfare.

There is no single general federal statute protecting engineers who report safety problems. OSHA administers the whistleblower and anti-retaliation provisions of 23 separate federal statutes, each covering particular industries and conduct, and each with its own filing deadline.

Under section 11(c)(2) of the Occupational Safety and Health Act, an employee who believes he has been discriminated against must file a complaint with the Secretary of Labor within 30 days after the violation occurs; complaints filed later are ordinarily presumed untimely, and tolling is available only on recognized equitable principles or in strongly extenuating circumstances.

The Rogers Commission concluded that the cause of the Challenger accident was a combustion gas leak through the right Solid Rocket Motor aft field joint, initiated at or shortly after ignition, which weakened or penetrated the External Tank and initiated vehicle structural breakup; contributing conditions included a launch temperature of 36 degrees Fahrenheit — 15 degrees colder than any previous flight — with the aft field joint's coldest point near 28 degrees Fahrenheit, reduced O-ring resiliency, joint gap opening within roughly 600 milliseconds of ignition, and the behaviour of the zinc chromate putty.

In the January 27, 1986 teleconference, Thiokol engineers including Roger Boisjoly presented O-ring erosion and blow-by data and recommended against launching outside the temperature database, whose low point was 53 degrees Fahrenheit; after an off-net management caucus, Thiokol reversed its engineering recommendation and Joe Kilminster signed and transmitted a recommendation to launch. The Commission found a serious flaw in the decision-making process, found that the waiving of launch constraints appears to have been at the expense of flight safety, and concluded that Thiokol management reversed its position at the urging of Marshall and contrary to the views of its engineers in order to accommodate a major customer. Senior NASA Level I and Level II officials testified that they did not know of the Thiokol objections.

The O-ring joint problem was documented internally well before the accident: on July 31, 1985 Boisjoly wrote to Thiokol's Vice President of Engineering that a field-joint failure would be a catastrophe of the highest order involving loss of human life, and a further internal memo in October 1985 protested that the seal task force was being delayed. Marshall imposed a launch constraint in July 1985 that was then waived for each subsequent flight, and entries incorrectly showing the problem closed kept it from surfacing in the 51-L Flight Readiness Review. The temperature correlation was obscured because reviewers plotted only the flights that had experienced O-ring distress.

The National Bureau of Standards found that the most probable cause of the July 17, 1981 Hyatt Regency walkways collapse in Kansas City, which left 113 people dead and 186 injured, was insufficient load capacity of the box beam-hanger rod connections, with failure initiating at the connection on the east end of the fourth floor walkway's middle box beam.

NBS identified two contributing factors at Hyatt Regency: inadequacy of the original box beam-hanger rod connection design, which was identical for all three walkways, and a change in hanger rod arrangement during construction from one continuous rod set to two sets, which essentially doubled the load on the fourth floor connections. NBS concluded the maximum load on a fourth floor connection at the time of collapse was only 31 percent of the ultimate capacity expected of a connection designed under the Kansas City Building Code, and that without the rod change the ultimate capacity would have been approximately 60 percent of that expected under the code — meaning the original design was already deficient.

NHTSA recall campaign 78V143000, received June 19, 1978, covers Ford Pinto model years including 1971 through 1976 and describes a fuel system defect in which a rear impact could disconnect the fuel filler pipe from the tank or puncture the forward face of the tank, resulting in fuel leakage.

In Grimshaw v. Ford Motor Co., 119 Cal.App.3d 757 (Cal. Ct. App. May 29, 1981), arising from a May 28, 1972 rear impact at roughly 28 to 37 miles per hour, the court recited evidence that the Pinto's fuel tank sat behind the rear axle with only about 9 or 10 inches of crush space, that Ford's own preproduction crash tests showed fuel system failure at speeds as low as about 21 miles per hour, and that feasible remedies existed at a few dollars per car. The jury awarded Grimshaw $2,516,000 compensatory and $125 million punitive damages; the punitive award was conditionally reduced to $3.5 million.

A separate criminal prosecution of Ford Motor Company for reckless homicide in Elkhart County, Indiana, arising from a 1978 Pinto fire, ended in a jury verdict of not guilty on all three counts in 1980.

The popular account in which a Ford cost-benefit memo is said to have driven a decision not to fix the Pinto is contested in the scholarly literature, which has treated demythologizing the case as an explicit project and has separated legal judgments from conclusions about moral wrongdoing.

NHTSA's July 26, 2001 rulemaking notice records that on August 9, 2000 Firestone announced a recall of ATX, ATX II, and Wilderness tires after complaints that the tread on these tires was separating, and that NHTSA had at that point attributed 203 deaths and more than 700 injuries to crashes involving tread separations on these tires.

Congress enacted the Transportation Recall Enhancement, Accountability, and Documentation (TREAD) Act on November 1, 2000, Public Law 106-414, in response to the Firestone recall; section 13 of the act mandated a rulemaking requiring a warning system to indicate to the driver when a tire is significantly underinflated.

EPA issued a notice of violation to Volkswagen on September 18, 2015 covering 2.0 litre diesel engines in model years 2009 through 2015 and a second notice on November 2, 2015 covering 3.0 litre engines in model years 2009 through 2016, involving approximately 590,000 vehicles; the software detected when a vehicle was undergoing emissions testing and turned full emissions controls on only during the test, with on-road nitrogen oxide emissions reaching up to 40 times the standard for the 2.0 litre vehicles.

On January 11, 2017 Volkswagen AG agreed to plead guilty to three criminal felony counts and to pay a $2.8 billion criminal penalty and $1.5 billion in civil penalties, $4.3 billion in total, arising from the use of a defeat device to cheat on emissions tests required by EPA and the California Air Resources Board.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the Hyatt Regency collapse is attributable solely to the connection change made during construction.
positions: The widely repeated account treats the fabricator's substitution of two rod sets for one continuous rod as the sole cause, implying the original detail was sound.

NBS BSS 143 identifies two contributing factors and states that without the rod change the ultimate capacity would still have been only about 60 percent of that expected under the Kansas City Building Code.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows NBS: the original connection design was already deficient, and the construction change roughly doubled the load at the fourth floor connections, taking a deficient detail to about 31 percent of code-expected capacity. Both facts are stated.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a Ford cost-benefit memo drove a decision not to fix the Ford Pinto.
positions: The popular narrative treats a 1973 Ford cost-benefit analysis as an internal Pinto go/no-go document that priced human lives against a fuel-tank fix.

Scholarly reassessment has treated the standard narrative as a myth requiring demythologizing and has distinguished legal liability findings from conclusions about moral blame; the primary document at issue was a submission in a federal fuel-system rulemaking rather than a Pinto-specific design decision record.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports only what the primary record supports — NHTSA's 1978 recall and the Grimshaw court's recitation of Ford's own crash test results, crush space, and low-cost remedies — and explicitly flags the cost-benefit-memo narrative as contested, telling students not to repeat it as established fact. The lesson does not assert the memo's contents, because the copy located (a scanned PDF hosted by the Center for Auto Safety) had no machine-readable text layer and could not be read in this research pass, and the leading law review reassessment (Gary T. Schwartz, 'The Myth of the Ford Pinto Case', 43 Rutgers L. Rev. 1013) sits behind a subscription database. Neither is cited as a source record.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How responsibility for the Firestone tread separation deaths divides between the tire and the vehicle it was fitted to.
positions: The federal action documented in the sources used here was directed at the tires.
The relative contribution of vehicle design, load, and the recommended inflation pressure was argued publicly at the time and is not resolved by the NHTSA material cited here.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the recall, the fatality and injury counts NHTSA attributed as of July 2001, and the TREAD Act response, and says plainly that the allocation of responsibility between tire and vehicle is not settled by the sources cited. NHTSA's Engineering Analysis Report and Initial Decision for EA00-023 could not be retrieved in this pass — nhtsa.gov, one.nhtsa.gov, and icsw.nhtsa.gov all returned HTTP 403 to the fetcher — so no claim is made about its specific conclusions.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft asserted nothing substantive about engineering ethics at all; its body text was subject-agnostic boilerplate ('Engineering Ethics is a concept students use to organize information...') that no source supports and that would be equally true of any noun.
The draft's Eli-10 analogy ('a label on a toolbox drawer') carried no content about the paramountcy principle and had no statement of the analogy's limits.
The draft's vocabulary list defined 'Engineering Ethics' circularly as 'a foundational Engineering Fundamentals concept covered in this lesson'.
The draft's question bank tested generic study skills rather than any verifiable fact about engineering ethics.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generated draft with researched content built on the codes themselves and on the primary investigation record.
Corrected the common Hyatt Regency account by stating the NBS finding that the original connection design was already inadequate, not merely the construction change.
Flagged the Ford Pinto cost-benefit-memo narrative as contested rather than repeating it, and limited the Pinto material to the NHTSA recall record and the Grimshaw court's factual recitation.

Stated that the Rogers Commission's finding was about a decision-making process that filtered out engineering doubt, and named the specific mechanisms it identified (waived launch constraints, erroneous closure entries, plotting only distressed flights against temperature) rather than the shorthand 'management ignored engineers'.

Replaced any implication that professional codes are legally enforceable in themselves with the accurate account: societies sanction members, state licensing boards regulate the right to practise, and the ASCE code disclaims setting a standard of care.
Gave an honest account of whistleblower protection as a 23-statute patchwork with short, statute-specific deadlines rather than implying a general legal shield exists.
Added explicit statements that the lesson is educational material, gives no legal or professional advice, takes no position on any current controversy, and is not engineering design guidance.
rightsIssues: The NSPE Code of Ethics for Engineers, the ASCE Code of Ethics, and other professional codes are copyrighted (the NSPE PDF carries an explicit all-rights-reserved notice). They are recorded as REFERENCE_ONLY. No code text is reproduced anywhere in the lesson; every description of a code provision is an original restatement of what the provision governs.

Rogers Commission report chapters, NBS Building Science Series 143, EPA pages and news releases, the Federal Register notice, the eCFR section, whistleblowers.gov, and the NHTSA recalls API are United States Government works and are treated as public domain; even so, the lesson restates rather than copies.

Grimshaw v. Ford Motor Co. is a judicial opinion and not itself copyrightable, but the copy actually read was a commercial republication (FindLaw); it is recorded REFERENCE_ONLY and only the court's factual findings are restated.

Becker et al. (2002) and Danley (2005) are subscription journal articles; only their bibliographic records and abstracts were read, and they are cited only for the existence and outcome of the Indiana prosecution and for the existence of a scholarly reassessment of the Pinto narrative.
The 1973 Ford memo hosted by the Center for Auto Safety was downloaded but is a scan with no text layer; it was not read and is not cited.

sourceRecords.title: NSPE Code of Ethics for Engineers
sourceRecords.notes: Existing registry id and URL reused exactly. Two-page PDF, publication #1102, marked as revised July 2019, carrying an explicit NSPE all-rights-reserved notice. Read in full by downloading the PDF with curl and extracting text with pypdf, because the NSPE HTML page returns HTTP 403 to the fetcher. Supports the six Fundamental Canons and their ordering, the Rules of Practice on paramountcy, competence, truthful public statements, faithful agency and conflicts, and deception, and the Professional Obligations on honesty, refusing to seal nonconforming work and withdrawing, avoiding deception of the public, confidentiality of client and employer business affairs and technical processes, conflicting interests, and the encouragement to adhere to sustainable development with its accompanying definition. Also supports the code's own statement that state registration board rules of professional conduct remain in full force and effect. No code text is reproduced in the lesson.

sourceRecords.title: ASCE Code of Ethics
sourceRecords.notes: Official ASCE PDF of the code, downloaded with curl and read in full with pypdf; the asce.org landing page did not render for the fetcher. Supports the five stakeholder groups in stated priority order (society; natural and built environment; profession; clients and employers; peers), the statement that responsibility 1a takes precedence over all other responsibilities, the footnote disclaiming that the code establishes a standard of care, the sustainable development and environmental obligations under the second stakeholder, and the client-and-employer duties covering conflicts disclosure, timely communication of risks, presenting consequences when engineering judgment is overruled, confidentiality of identified proprietary information, competence, and sealing only work prepared or reviewed under responsible charge. No code text is reproduced in the lesson.

sourceRecords.title: Report of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident, Volume 1, Chapter VI: An Accident Rooted in History
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the pre-accident documentary record: Boisjoly's July 31, 1985 memo to Thiokol's Vice President of Engineering warning that a field joint failure would be a catastrophe of the highest order involving loss of human life, the October 1985 memo protesting delays to the seal task force, the July 1985 Marshall launch constraint and its repeated waiver, the erroneous problem-report entries indicating the O-ring issue was closed, and the reviewers' practice of plotting only flights that had experienced O-ring distress against temperature, which obscured the correlation.

sourceRecords.title: Investigation of the Kansas City Hyatt Regency Walkways Collapse, NBS Building Science Series 143
sourceRecords.notes: 378-page report downloaded with curl (too large for the fetcher) and read via pypdf text extraction of the abstract, executive summary, and introduction. Supports the July 17, 1981 collapse date and time, the 113 dead and 186 injured figures, the three-walkway suspension arrangement, the conclusion that the most probable cause was insufficient load capacity of the box beam-hanger rod connections with failure initiating at the east end of the fourth floor middle box beam, the two contributing factors (inadequate original design plus the construction change to two rod sets), the 31 percent and approximately 60 percent capacity figures relative to the Kansas City Building Code, and the finding that from the day of construction the walkways had only minimal capacity to resist their own weight.

sourceRecords.title: Whistleblower Statutes, OSHA Whistleblower Protection Program
sourceRecords.provider: Occupational Safety and Health Administration, U.S. Department of Labor
sourceRecords.notes: Supports that OSHA enforces the whistleblower provisions of 23 separate federal statutes spanning transportation, consumer product and food safety, environmental laws (Clean Air Act, CERCLA, Federal Water Pollution Control Act, Safe Drinking Water Act, Solid Waste Disposal Act, Toxic Substances Control Act), nuclear and energy (Energy Reorganization Act), and financial and health-insurance areas, and that each law requires complaints to be filed within a specified number of days after the alleged retaliation. Individual deadline values are not listed on this page; the 30-day OSH Act figure used in the lesson comes from the eCFR record instead.

sourceRecords.title: 29 CFR 1977.15 — Filing of complaint for discrimination (OSH Act section 11(c))
sourceRecords.provider: Office of the Federal Register / eCFR
sourceRecords.notes: Read via the eCFR renderer API after the ecfr.gov page redirected the fetcher. Supports that section 11(c)(2) allows an employee to file within 30 days after the violation occurs, that complaints not filed within 30 days are ordinarily presumed untimely, and that tolling is available only on recognized equitable principles or in strongly extenuating circumstances such as employer concealment or a continuing violation — and expressly not merely because grievance-arbitration proceedings are pending.

sourceRecords.title: Licensure
sourceRecords.notes: Existing registry id and URL reused exactly from the merged what-engineers-do topic. Read with curl. Cited here only for the narrow point that professional engineering licensure is administered by state and territorial licensing boards and exists so that individuals practise in a manner that protects the health, safety, and welfare of the public.
